title: Fused-Planes: Why Train a Thousand Tri-Planes When You Can Share?
primary_area: applications to computer vision, audio, language, and other modalities

response.summary: The paper proposes Fused-Planes, a tri-plane representation decomposed into object-specific micro planes and weighted combinations of shared base planes, trained jointly with a latent-image autoencoder. The approach is practically motivated and reports substantial savings over independently trained tri-planes, but the novelty is moderate and several evaluation/accounting issues weaken the headline conclusions.
strengths: The micro/macro decomposition is simple, intuitive, and preserves a planar representation while exploiting dataset-level sharing (pp. 4–5).

Experiments cover several ShapeNet categories, faces, multi-class training, quality/resource metrics, and relevant component ablations; the full model improves substantially over the tri-plane baseline in speed and often in quality (pp. 7–10).
The appendix provides useful implementation details, total-cost tables, memory breakdowns, rendering-speed results, and qualitative examples (pp. 15–33).
weaknesses: Headline per-object memory reductions exclude 360–384 MB of shared components. At the actual 2,000-object scale, total memory is about 1.3 GB versus 2.9 GB for Tri-Planes, far less than the advertised 3.2× per-object reduction; the 1875× ULW claim is likewise not representative of total deployment cost (pp. 16, 20).

The training description is internally concerning: regime 2 continues updating shared base planes, renderer, and decoder without revisiting the first 500 objects, potentially changing their reconstructions; this also conflicts with the claim that additional objects can use frozen shared components. The regime tables do not clearly rule out forgetting (pp. 6, 15–17, 33).

Evidence is limited to synthetic, bounded, low-resolution object-centric data, with unclear evaluation-set sizes beyond four per-object examples, no variability across runs, and no demonstration that the learned planes retain practical compatibility or performance in a downstream 2D-model pipeline (pp. 7–10, 16, 24–30).
response.score_rationale: The work offers a useful efficiency-oriented engineering contribution with promising empirical results, but dictionary-style shared factors plus latent rendering is only moderately novel. More importantly, shared-cost accounting, possible regime-2 interference, and limited synthetic evaluation leave central efficiency and robustness claims insufficiently established. I therefore rate it marginally below acceptance, with some uncertainty because clarification of the training protocol could alleviate a major concern.

response.summary: The paper proposes a shared dictionary of macro tri-planes combined with per-object micro planes and joint latent-space rendering. The approach is coherent and reports substantial efficiency improvements, but the novelty is primarily a combination of low-rank/shared representations and latent NeRF training, while the evidence is too narrow to fully substantiate its broad scalability and compatibility claims.
strengths: The micro/macro decomposition is simple, clearly specified, and preserves a tri-planar representation; the joint latent-space objective is technically plausible (pp. 4–6).
Reported gains over Tri-Planes are substantial in training time, storage, and rendering speed, with total-cost scaling also provided rather than only per-object numbers (pp. 7, 18–20).
Ablations address the latent space, shared macro component, number of bases, multi-class training, and VAE initialization, generally supporting the main design choices (pp. 8–9, 17–19).
weaknesses: Headline per-object memory excludes 360–384 MB of shared components, making claims such as the 1875× ULW reduction potentially misleading outside the asymptotic regime; the total-memory advantage at 2,000 objects is materially smaller (pp. 16, 20).

Evaluation is confined to synthetic, bounded, 128×128 object-centric data and held-out views of reconstructed objects. There is no demonstrated unseen-object adaptation, real-scene evaluation, or downstream image-model experiment validating the claimed practical compatibility (pp. 8, 10, 16).

Statistical support is weak: no variability across runs is reported, and the appendix exposes only four evaluated examples per category. Moreover, regime 2 continues updating shared bases and the decoder without revisiting the first 500 objects, creating a forgetting/staleness concern that the small regime comparison does not conclusively resolve (pp. 15, 17, 24–25, 33).
response.score_rationale: The method is useful and empirically promising, but moderately incremental and supported by a restricted evaluation with ambiguous memory framing and unresolved sequential-training concerns. I therefore place it marginally below acceptance; uncertainty remains because the supplied results may understate evaluation-set size and the regime tables may have been measured after all training.

response.summary: The paper proposes Fused-Planes, which factorizes per-object tri-planes into object-specific micro planes and weighted combinations of shared base planes, while jointly learning a latent image space. It reports strong storage and training-time improvements on synthetic object-centric reconstruction, but the methodological novelty is incremental and several central efficiency and compatibility claims are not fully isolated or validated.
strengths: The micro/macro decomposition is simple, intuitive, and preserves a materializable tri-planar structure; the ultra-lightweight variant offers a practically interesting storage trade-off (pp. 4–5, 20).
Experiments cover four ShapeNet categories, faces, multi-class training, three reconstruction metrics, qualitative results, resource scaling, and relevant architectural ablations (pp. 7–10, 17–25).

Within the reported setup, the full model substantially improves efficiency over RGB Tri-Planes while retaining or improving average quality, and total-memory accounting is eventually provided rather than only per-object storage (pp. 7, 19–20).
weaknesses: The attribution of the headline speedup is unclear: much of it comes from rendering low-resolution latent images with a pretrained Stable-Diffusion VAE, while the latent-only micro ablation is already much faster than RGB Tri-Planes. A direct comparison to the cited latent-NeRF training method under matched settings is missing (pp. 5, 8–10).

Efficiency accounting is potentially misleading. Headline memory excludes 360–384 MB of shared components, and reported per-object/total training figures are not consistently explained; pretrained-VAE cost is also excluded. For example, the 8.96-minute figure on p. 7 does not directly reconcile with the 14.5-day total for 2,000 objects on p. 19.

Evidence is restricted to synthetic, bounded, 128×128 object-centric data with many training views, and no claimed downstream compatibility with existing 2D pipelines is demonstrated. Moreover, shared bases, renderer, and decoder continue changing in regime 2, but possible degradation of earlier objects or true incremental addition is not rigorously assessed (pp. 15–16, 31–33).
response.score_rationale: The method is useful and the empirical gains within its chosen setting are substantial, supporting borderline acceptance. However, the core idea is a fairly standard shared dictionary/factorization combined with latent rendering, and the paper does not convincingly disentangle these sources of gain or validate its broader compatibility and scalability claims. I therefore rate it marginally below acceptance; uncertainty remains because reproducibility could clarify the timing protocol.

response.summary: The paper proposes Fused-Planes, combining a shared dictionary of macro tri-planes, object-specific micro planes, and a jointly trained latent image space to amortize reconstruction across object collections. The approach is simple but practically useful, with strong reported efficiency and generally competitive planar-representation quality. I am marginally positive, although the novelty is incremental and several efficiency and evaluation claims need more careful qualification.
strengths: Substantial practical gains are reported against Tri-Planes: roughly 7.2× faster per-object training and improved average NVS quality, with a clear quality–storage trade-off through the ULW variant (pp. 7–9).

The paper includes useful component ablations, multi-class experiments, base-count studies, rendering-speed measurements, and memory breakdowns, which broadly support the design choices (pp. 8–10, 17–20).
The representation retains a fixed planar tensor form while exploiting cross-object structure, addressing a relevant cost in constructing large tri-plane collections (pp. 4–5).
weaknesses: The headline memory reductions exclude 360–384 MB of shared components. At 2,000 objects, the reported total memory is about 1.3 GB versus 2.9 GB for Tri-Planes, much less dramatic than the 3.2× per-object claim; ULW’s 1875× claim is likewise a marginal-storage rather than total-system comparison (pp. 16, 20).

Novelty is moderate: the central mechanism is essentially dictionary factorization of planar features plus an existing latent-NeRF strategy. The claimed compatibility with downstream image-based tri-plane pipelines is not experimentally demonstrated, despite being a primary motivation (pp. 2–5, 7–10).

Evaluation is confined to low-resolution synthetic, bounded object-centric data, with only four per-object cases shown per category and no uncertainty estimates. Moreover, regime 2 continues updating shared bases, renderer, and decoder without revisiting regime-1 objects, leaving potential drift of the first 500 representations insufficiently explained (pp. 16–17, 24–25, 33).
response.score_rationale: The method offers credible and valuable amortized efficiency with solid ablations, supporting a marginally-above-acceptance score. However, the incremental technical contribution, amortization-dependent headline claims, limited evaluation breadth, and ambiguity around sequential shared-component updates prevent a stronger recommendation.

response.summary: The paper proposes Fused-Planes, a tri-plane representation combining shared basis planes with object-specific residual planes and training in a jointly adapted latent image space. The idea is simple and practically motivated, and the reported efficiency/quality trade-off is promising. However, the headline memory claims rely on excluding substantial shared components, the two-stage optimization raises an unresolved stability issue, and evaluation is limited to low-resolution synthetic object-centric reconstruction without validating the claimed downstream compatibility.
strengths: The micro/macro decomposition is conceptually clear, preserves a fixed planar representation, and offers a useful scalable design for exploiting class-level redundancy (pp. 4–5).

Reported results show strong marginal per-object efficiency while generally matching or improving Tri-Planes in reconstruction quality across several categories, with relevant component ablations (pp. 7–9).
The appendix provides unusually extensive reporting, including total-resource scaling, rendering speed, memory breakdowns, hyperparameters, and qualitative/per-object results (pp. 17–33).
weaknesses: The headline 3.2× and 1875× memory reductions concern marginal per-object storage and exclude 360–384 MB of shared components (p. 16). At 2,000 objects, the disclosed total costs are 1.3 GB and 0.4 GB versus 2.9 GB for Tri-Planes—useful, but far smaller gains than the headline framing suggests (p. 20).

In regime 2, the algorithm continues updating shared base planes, renderer, and decoder while no longer revisiting the first 500 objects (pp. 15, 32–33). This can invalidate their frozen object-specific parameters; Tables 6–7 do not clearly evaluate those first objects after all shared-component updates, leaving final-set stability uncertain (p. 17).

Evidence is confined to 128×128 synthetic/object-centric datasets, and no downstream image-model task tests the central compatibility motivation (pp. 6–8, 16). Novelty is also moderate: the main construction is a shared linear dictionary plus per-object residual, combined with prior latent-NeRF machinery.
response.score_rationale: The paper presents a sensible, well-explained efficiency method with promising results and substantial supplementary analysis. Nevertheless, incomplete validation of joint-training stability, potentially misleading headline memory accounting, and narrow evaluation prevent a confident acceptance recommendation. I therefore rate it marginally below acceptance; uncertainty remains because the supplied text does not allow verification of code or timing measurements.
